script:
Hello, this is The Portfolio Podcast for SOXX. Tuesday — here is your SOXX recap. The portfolio closed five point three five percent down on the session.

Semiconductors are selling off hard, and the pressure is not selective. Nine of ten primary holdings finished in the red Tuesday, with losses concentrated in memory, equipment, and AI-adjacent names. The breadth of the decline is what demands attention.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average extended its advance for a third session, adding roughly five hundred points as strength in defensive and non-technology sectors offset the chip rout. The divergence is sharp — the Nasdaq moved lower as semiconductor names dragged it down, with analysts at multiple desks describing the chip selling as, quote, indiscriminate, unquote, per Fortune.

The top story Tuesday belongs to Micron Technology, and the numbers are difficult to ignore. Micron fell eight point eight five percent on the session, closing as one of the worst performers on the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, according to reporting from Yahoo Finance. The move was not company-specific — there was no earnings miss, no guidance cut, no product failure. Instead, Micron absorbed the full weight of a sector-wide selloff driven by intensifying anxiety over AI spending sustainability. Analysts have characterized the pressure as a repricing of AI-linked growth expectations broadly, with memory names bearing disproportionate damage given their sensitivity to data center demand cycles. For this portfolio, Micron sits as the second-largest primary holding at eight point zero eight percent of total weight. A session decline of nearly nine percent from a position of that size carries meaningful drag. The question holders are watching is whether this is valuation compression or the beginning of a demand narrative shift.

Advanced Micro Devices was down eight point one five percent on the session. Despite the steep decline, there was a constructive development worth noting. Core Scientific, the bitcoin mining company transitioning toward AI infrastructure, reported a major partnership with Advanced Micro Devices centered on Instinct graphics processing units, with Core Scientific shares jumping eleven percent on the news. Additionally, Qisda Group's AEWIN division launched a new server portfolio built around Advanced Micro Devices EPYC nine thousand series server processors. The AI infrastructure buildout is ongoing — the stock price and the deal flow are moving in opposite directions Tuesday, and that tension is the story to watch.

Turning to Nvidia, which was the lone bright spot in the primary holdings. Nvidia finished up zero point two five percent on the session — a modest gain, but meaningful given the severity of selling elsewhere in the sector. Fortune noted the chip slump has created what one analyst called, quote, a lot of panic around the AI investment, unquote. Nvidia's relative resilience suggests the market is drawing some distinction between GPU leadership and the broader semiconductor complex.

Over at Broadcom, the stock was down zero point six zero percent. Separately, news around Qualcomm's expanded Samsung partnership and AI infrastructure push offers a read-through for custom silicon demand broadly — a theme Broadcom continues to be positioned around. Watch for any AI ASIC commentary heading into the next earnings cycle.

Intel was down five point eight six percent on the session. The loss adds to a difficult stretch for Intel as it navigates its foundry repositioning. No company-specific catalyst drove Tuesday's move — sector pressure was the primary factor.

Applied Materials fell seven point eight two percent. Equipment names were among the hardest hit Tuesday, and Applied Materials was no exception. The stock's sensitivity to fab spending cycles makes it a direct read on whether the AI capital expenditure wave is being questioned.

Meanwhile, KLA Corporation dropped six point one eight percent. KLA is scheduled to report earnings after Tuesday's close, which makes the session move worth contextualizing carefully — pre-earnings positioning and broad semiconductor selling combined for a difficult session.

Marvell Technology was down seven point seven seven percent on the session. Like Applied Materials, the decline appears sector-driven rather than news-specific. Custom AI chip demand remains the core long-term thesis for Marvell, with no new developments surfacing Tuesday.

Lam Research fell seven point five four percent. Lam's exposure to memory and advanced logic equipment makes it vulnerable in sessions where both memory names and AI sentiment are under simultaneous pressure. That was precisely Tuesday's setup.

Finally, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company was down one point seven zero percent — the smallest decline among the primary holdings outside of Nvidia. Taiwan Semiconductor's relative strength reflects its position as foundational infrastructure across the entire semiconductor ecosystem, with demand diversification providing some buffer against single-theme selling.

Three items to track in the next forty-eight hours. First, KLA Corporation's earnings report — already referenced, results are due after Tuesday's close, and commentary on equipment demand will set tone for the equipment names in this portfolio. Second, the Federal Reserve policy decision — markets are watching for any rate surprise this week, which carries direct implications for growth and technology valuations. Third, SK Hynix earnings — as a major memory competitor to Micron, SK Hynix's results and forward guidance will serve as a critical data point for assessing whether memory demand is softening or holding.

This is The Portfolio Podcast for SOXX. We will be back same time the next business day with tomorrow's news. The Federal Reserve decision and KLA's earnings call are the two events that will define the tone heading into Wednesday's open.
